# Mahācattārīsaka Sutta (MN 117 (PTS MN iii 71))

**ID:** MN 117 (PTS MN iii 71)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahācattārīsaka Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Great Forty
**PTS:** MN iii 71
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn117
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahācattārīsaka Sutta* (MN 117; PTS MN iii 71–78), translated as "The Great Forty", is a fundamental discourse on noble right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*) and its prerequisites [SuttaCentral; Segall 2003; Jantrasrisalai 2008]. Unlike discourses that define right concentration strictly through the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), MN 117 defines it as mental unification equipped with the other seven factors of the noble eightfold path [Anālayo 2003; Anālayo 2011]. Throughout the discourse, right view is given a leading role, working in constant cooperation with right effort and right mindfulness to monitor and correct mental states [Anālayo 2003; Anālayo 2011; Anālayo 2014]. The discourse is distinctive within the four Pāli Nikāyas for dividing path factors into two levels: a mundane (*lokiya*) level accompanied by defilements and ripening in merit, and a supramundane, noble (*lokuttara*) level [Jantrasrisalai 2008; Bodhi 2005; Anālayo 2011]. The noble eightfold path ultimately culminates in the tenfold path of the arahant by adding right knowledge (*sammāñāṇa*) and right liberation (*sammāvimutti*) [Anālayo 2014].

Scholars have noted that the supramundane exposition employs technical definitions and expressions—such as *appanā* ("fixing" of the mind) and *cetaso abhiniropanā* ("application" or "inclination of the mind")—that are virtually absent from the early discourses and characteristic of the Abhidhamma and commentarial strata [Anālayo 2003; Anālayo 2010; Anālayo 2011]. Comparison with early parallels suggests that this supramundane treatment may have originated as an explanatory gloss that was later integrated into the canonical Pali text [Anālayo 2010; Anālayo 2011]. The doctrinal prominence of MN 117 is underscored by the commentarial term *mahācattālīsakabhāṇaka* (or *mahācattārīsakabhāṇaka*) found in the *Sammohavinodanī*, reflecting either a specialized reciter or a formal inquiry into whether a monk knew the exposition of this sutta [Adikaram 1946; Anālayo 2010; Anālayo 2011]. The discourse is also cited in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 1.6) [SuttaCentral].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include a Sarvāstivāda version in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 189), a Mūlasarvāstivāda discourse citation in Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā* (Up 6.080) preserved in Tibetan, a Sanskrit fragment (SHT sutta 51), Chinese *Saṃyukta-āgama* discourses (SĀ 785, SĀ 784), and Pali parallels at AN 4.30 and SN 22.62 [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2011]. Computational text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus indicates extensive Pali-internal sharing (1,729 matching passages across 112 texts), with the highest volume in the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Magga Saṃyutta* (SN 45) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments in DharmaNexus corroborate the curated parallels, showing prominent matches with the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26) and *Saṃyukta-āgama* (T 99), the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (D 4094), and Sanskrit and Tibetan versions of the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* [DharmaNexus].
